questions.q: What is a login, precisely, in SQL Server's security model?
options: A server-level principal that authenticates to the instance but grants no database access by itself
A database-level object that grants table access
A synonym for a Windows user account with no relation to SQL Server
A fixed server role
questions.explain: A login is a server-scoped principal. It gets you authenticated to the instance; a separate database user is required for any database access.

questions.q: Which statement creates a SQL Server login (not a Windows-authenticated one) that enforces Windows password-complexity rules?
options: CREATE LOGIN app_svc WITH PASSWORD = 'Str0ng!Pass', CHECK_POLICY = ON;
CREATE LOGIN [DOMAIN\app_svc] FROM WINDOWS;
CREATE USER app_svc FOR LOGIN app_svc;
ALTER SERVER ROLE sysadmin ADD MEMBER app_svc;
questions.explain: CREATE LOGIN ... WITH PASSWORD creates a SQL Server login; CHECK_POLICY = ON ties it to the Windows password-complexity policy.

questions.q: Where does SQL Server expose metadata about every login and server role on the instance?
options: sys.server_principals
sys.database_principals
sys.objects
sys.dm_exec_sessions
questions.explain: sys.server_principals is the catalog view for server-scoped principals: logins, Windows users/groups, and server roles.

questions.q: A SQL login connects successfully but every query against a database fails with a permission error rather than a login-failure error. What does that pattern indicate?
options: The login exists and authenticated, but no database user maps it into that database
The login's password is wrong
The instance is in Windows Authentication mode
The login has been dropped
questions.explain: A login-failure error means authentication itself failed; a permission error after a successful connection means the login is missing the database-user mapping that grants it access inside that specific database.

questions.q: What does CREATE LOGIN [DOMAIN\DBAs] FROM WINDOWS accomplish?
options: It maps an existing Windows/AD group to a SQL Server login, so any member of that group can authenticate
It creates a brand-new Active Directory group named DBAs
It grants sysadmin to everyone in the DBAs group automatically
It creates a database user, not a login
questions.explain: FROM WINDOWS maps an existing Windows or AD identity — a user or a group — to a server-level login; it does not create the AD object or grant any permission beyond authentication.
